title: I built an AI research agent for crypto that checks live market data before it answers
author: Kind-Economics-7184

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: when it backtests the RSI alert on past candles, does it show how many times the signal fired?

replies.author: Kind-Economics-7184
replies.body:
Yes. Before it offers to create the alert, it runs the exact rule over the last 1,000 candles of each coin (on the 4h that's roughly 5–6 months) and shows you:

\- how many times it fired, per coin, on a chart with a marker at every spot

\- how often you'd actually get the alert (e.g. "≈ 3 / month"). It's counted with the alert's cooldown, so a condition that stays true for days isn't counted 20 times

\- what price did afterwards: how often it was higher a few hours, a day and a few days later, and the average move compared with the coin's normal drift over the same period, so a bull run doesn't make every rule look good

If the rule fired fewer than 10 times it tells you to treat the numbers as anecdotes, and if it never fired it won't offer the alert at all.

It's a look at the past, not a promise about the next signal.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: the ≈3 a month next to the chart markers is useful, most alert tools never tell you how often you'll get pinged. 1,000 candles on the 4h is mostly one regime though, half a year of one direction can make a reversal rule look better than it is.

replies.author: Kind-Economics-7184
replies.body:
Fair point, and it made me go back to the numbers. The edge on the card was already measured against the same window's baseline (just holding over those same bars), so a steady trend doesn't inflate it on its own, and this window wasn't one-way (BTC about flat, coins above their 200-candle average \~55% of the time).

But you're right about the part that matters: an oversold rule fires almost only in down phases (85–90% of its alerts on the top 40 coins came below the 200 average), so the pooled number says little about how it does in an uptrend. Some rules even flip: a lower Bollinger touch had a +1.2% edge over 3 days below the 200 average and −0.8% above it.

So the backtest now splits every alert by whether the coin was above or below its own 200-candle average when it fired, shows the edge for each side on the card ("too few" when a side has under 10 alerts), and flags it when the edge flips or the alerts pile up on one side. The agent gets the same split, so it can say when an edge only shows up in one kind of market. Thanks, good catch.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: measuring against holding the same bars answers most of it. what I'd still watch is how often the signal fired in that window, since a handful of fires can beat the hold on luck alone.
